slides.title: Chapter 10: Reading and Writing Files
slides.say: This chapter of the book, Reading and Writing Files, shows how a program names a file with a path, makes folders, reads and writes text, and keeps Python values between two runs. The deck has eighteen code examples that run on the chapter page, true stories about the people behind these tools, and a plain explanation of every concept. Each code slide shows one whole program in one box that can be copied in a single step, a balloon that explains it, and what the run really printed, drawn as a table, a chart or a small picture. The sample files a program needs are made by lines that the slide does not show. Slide 2 lays out the five parts, and chapter 11 continues with whole folders and archives.

slides.title: Today's route through five parts
slides.say: The table is the map of the chapter. Each row is one of the five parts, with the slides it covers, the number of code examples in it and the tools you will run. The last row covers the newer features of Python, the summary, the practice questions and the links. The same eighteen examples are listed in the Slide code tab of the chapter page, in this order, so a slide and its tab can be opened side by side. The parts build on each other: paths first, then folders, text, saved values and programs. Part 1 starts on slide 4.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions run through the chapter, and the deck comes back to them at the end. The first asks which tools only compute a path, which ask the file system a question and which change a file or a folder; the summary on slide 39 sorts them. The second asks where the book's printed output and programs differ from current Python; slide 37, the quiz files of Project 4, and slide 38, the newer features, answer it. Every tool of the chapter is one of the three kinds: compute, ask or change. Holding that sort in mind makes each later slide easier to place.

slides.title: Part 1: Filepaths
slides.say: Part 1 is about filepaths. A path names the place of a file, and pathlib turns that name into an object that you can join with a slash, ask where it starts and take apart. The four cards on the slide are the ideas of the part: the path object, the working directory, absolute and relative paths, and the parts of a path. Slides 5 to 10 cover them in code and in pictures, and the same ideas return in part 2, where paths are used to build folders and find files.

slides.title: Filepaths and how to join them
slides.say: The headline says what a filepath is: the list of folders to open, in order, with the file name at the end. The rows explain each idea in plain words. An absolute path starts at the root of the drive and names the same file wherever the program runs, while a relative path starts at the working directory and means something else when that directory changes. The slash operator joins names, and Path writes the separator of the computer that runs the program: a backslash on Windows and a slash on Linux and macOS. Slide 6 shows the same ideas in code, and slide 9 returns to absolute and relative paths.

slides.title: Path objects: joining names into a path
slides.say: Path() joins the names it is given with the separator of the computer and returns one path object, so the result prints with backslashes, as it does on Windows, where this book's examples run by default, and with slashes on Linux and macOS. The program shows three ways to write the same path: all the names inside Path(), the slash operator between names, and the slash between a Path and another Path; the three lines print the same text. The slash works only when a Path stands on its left side, because two plain strings cannot be divided. The last loop joins a folder name with each file name in a list. Slide 7 tells the story of the proposal that made paths objects, and slide 10 takes a path apart.

slides.title: Story: a 2012 proposal made paths objects
slides.say: On 30 July 2012 Antoine Pitrou, a Python core developer, wrote PEP 428, which proposed that a filesystem path should be an object with its own methods and not a plain string. The proposal went through the Python Enhancement Proposals process and shipped in Python 3.4 in March 2014. Before that, separate functions of the os.path module worked on strings and were clumsy and hard to read. Path('spam', 'bacon', 'eggs') and the slash operator of this chapter come from that proposal, and slide 6 uses both. The link on the slide leads to the proposal itself.

slides.title: The working directory and Path objects
slides.say: The headline defines the working directory: the folder from which every relative path is read. os.getcwd() and Path.cwd() return it, and os.chdir() changes it, after which the same relative path names a different place. Path.home() returns the home directory of the user who runs the program. Path() only builds a path object from text and does not look at the disk, so a path can name a file that does not exist. is_absolute tells whether a path starts at the root, and name, stem, suffix, parent and drive return its parts. Slide 9 runs these calls, and slide 10 takes a path apart.

slides.title: Where you stand: working directory and home
slides.say: Every running program has a current working directory, the folder that its relative paths start from. Path.cwd() returns it and Path.home() returns the home folder of the user; both are absolute paths, so the first two answers are True. A path written like spam/bacon/eggs has no start of its own, so it is relative and the third answer is False. The last line shows that a leading dot, which means the current folder, changes nothing: ./spam.txt and spam.txt are the same path. The names of the real folders differ from computer to computer, which is why the program prints yes-or-no answers and not the folders. Slide 10 takes a path apart.

slides.title: Taking a path apart
slides.say: A path is made of parts, and each part is an attribute of the path object. The drive is C:, the anchor is the drive with its separator, the parent is everything before the last name, the name is the last part with its ending, the stem is the name without the ending and the suffix is the ending alone. Parts gives all the names as a tuple, and parents[1] is the folder two levels up. The program uses PureWindowsPath so that a Windows path can be taken apart on any computer; on Windows the same lines work with Path. The table on the slide lists the parts as the run found them. Part 2 of the deck, on folders and files, begins with slide 11.

slides.title: Part 2: Folders and file facts
slides.say: Part 2 builds folders, finds files and asks the file system questions. makedirs and mkdir create folders, glob finds files by a pattern, and exists and stat tell you whether a path is there and how big and how old it is. Only makedirs and mkdir change the disk, by adding folders; glob, exists and stat only ask. The four cards on the slide give the ideas, and slides 12 to 15 show them in pictures and in code. Part 3 then opens files and starts to read and write the text inside them.

slides.title: Folders, file facts and glob patterns
slides.say: The headline explains the two ideas of this part. A folder holds files and other folders, and a glob pattern selects names with the wildcards * and ?. os.makedirs creates every missing folder on the way, while mkdir creates one folder and needs parents=True to create the missing ones above it. exists answers True or False without raising an error. stat returns the size in bytes and the times of change of a file, and glob lists the paths that match a pattern. Slides 13 to 15 turn each row into code.

slides.title: Creating folders and listing a tree
slides.say: Os.makedirs builds a whole chain of folders at once, here delicious, walnut and waffles, and creates the folders in the middle if they are missing. The Path method mkdir makes only the last folder of a path, here pecan inside walnut, and raises an error if the folder above it does not exist. The loop at the end walks through everything below delicious with rglob, in sorted order, and prints each path: walnut, then pecan, then waffles. The table on the slide draws the same tree. Both ways raise an error when the last folder already exists, unless exist_ok=True is given, which chapter 11 uses. Slide 14 finds files by a pattern.

slides.title: glob: find files by a pattern
slides.say: Glob finds files by a pattern. In a pattern, an asterisk stands for any number of characters and a question mark for exactly one. The folder holds project1.txt, project2.txt, project10.txt and notes.csv. The pattern *.txt finds the three text files, and sorted puts them in text order, which is why project10 comes before project2. The pattern project?.txt finds only project1 and project2, because project10 has two characters after the word project and the question mark allows just one. The table on the slide shows for each file which pattern takes it. Glob returns paths, so it can feed any loop. Slide 15 asks a path about its size and its time.

slides.title: Does it exist? How big? How old?
slides.say: A path can be asked about the file it points to. Exists says whether anything is there, is_file whether it is a file, and is_dir whether it is a folder; the file spam.txt gives True, True and False. Stat holds the details: st_size is the size in bytes, 13 for the text Hello, world!, and st_mtime is the time of the last change in seconds since 1970. The set-up gives the file a fixed time, so asctime with gmtime prints Tue Apr  9 01:45:29 2024 in universal time on every computer; the book prints the local time. A path that does not exist gives False and no error. Part 3 of the deck, on reading and writing, begins on slide 16.

slides.title: Part 3: Reading and writing text
slides.say: Part 3 is about reading and writing text. A file is opened, read or written, and closed again, and the with statement does the closing for you. The modes w, a and x decide what happens to text that is already in the file, and the encoding decides how letters become bytes. Slides 17 to 25 take these ideas in order, from whole-file calls to the cursor, with, modes and encoding. Part 4 then saves whole Python values instead of text.

slides.title: Opening, reading and closing files
slides.say: The headline gives the three steps of working with a file: open it, read or write, and close it, always in this order. A plaintext file holds characters and line breaks that an editor shows as they are, while a binary file holds bytes, such as a picture or a spreadsheet, that need the program made for them. open() takes a path and a mode and returns a file object, which remembers how far the program has read. read returns everything from that position to the end, and close ends the use of the file. Slides 18 to 21 run these steps.

slides.title: Whole files: write_text and read_text
slides.say: The shortest way to use a file is to write or read all of it in one call. Write_text saves a string in a file and returns the number of characters it wrote, here 13 for Hello, world!. Read_text returns the whole text of the file as a string. The Path object opens and closes the file by itself, so there is nothing to forget. The table on the slide shows what each call gave back. The method is a good fit for small text files; for a file that is too large to hold at once, or for reading line by line, the open function on the next slides is needed. Slide 19 tells the story of the character set behind these calls.

slides.title: Story: why Windows paths use a backslash
slides.say: In 1983 Microsoft released MS-DOS 2.0, the first version of DOS that could keep folders inside folders, and its programmers had to pick a character to separate the folder names in a path. They could not use the slash, because MS-DOS already used it in front of command options. The backslash was chosen instead, and every Windows path since then is written that way. Larry Osterman, an engineer at Microsoft, described the reason in a blog post in 2005, and writers on computer history still disagree about how much IBM's wish to keep the old commands working had to do with it. Slide 6 shows Path() joining names, and it hides the difference: Path() joins the names with the separator of the computer that runs the program. The link opens Osterman's post.

slides.title: open(): a file object you must close
slides.say: Open returns a file object, and a file object must be closed when the work is done. The first call uses mode w, which starts the file empty, and write returns the number of characters it wrote, 14. The second call uses mode a, which adds to the end, and writes 25 more. The third call opens the file for reading, read returns the whole content and the program prints it, both lines. The chart shows the two counts, and the file holds 39 bytes in all. Every open names the encoding UTF-8, so the text is read back as it was written. Forgetting to close can lose data; the with statement on slide 23 does the closing automatically.

slides.title: Reading: the file cursor moves
slides.say: A file object remembers the position it has read to. Readlines reads every line from the cursor to the end and returns them as a list, here four lines of the sonnet, each ending with a newline character. The program prints how many lines there are and the first line. After that the cursor stands at the end of the file, so the second read returns an empty string, shown as two quotation marks. A second read of the same file object therefore finds nothing unless the file is opened again. The table on the slide shows the three results. Slide 23 introduces the with statement.

slides.title: Writing files and the with block
slides.say: The headline explains the with block: it opens a file and closes it again when the block ends, even if an error stops the program inside the block. The rows give the writing modes: w starts with an empty file, a adds to the end and x refuses a file that already exists. write adds one string, write_text writes a whole string in one call, read_text returns the whole content and readlines returns a list of lines. A context manager is an object that sets up when the block starts and cleans up when it ends. Slides 23 and 24 show the with block and the modes.

slides.title: with: the file closes itself
slides.say: The with statement opens a file and closes it when its block ends, even if an error happens inside the block. The program writes a text in the first block and reads it back in the second. Inside the second block the variable content takes the text, and after the block the program prints it. The last line prints the closed attribute of the file object, which is True: the file is closed although the program never called close. The table shows both values. This is the form that current Python programs use, because the close call cannot be forgotten. Slide 24 compares the write modes.

slides.title: Write modes: w overwrites, a appends
slides.say: A file can be opened for writing in different modes, and the mode decides what happens to the content that is already there. Mode w starts the file again, so the old content is thrown away. Mode a keeps the old content and adds the new text at the end. The loop runs four steps: w writes A, a adds B, a adds C, and w writes D. After each step the program reads the file back. After the last step only D is left, because the second w erased A, B and C. The table lists the file after each step. A third mode, x, creates a new file and refuses if the file exists; it is not part of this program. Slide 25 shows how the bytes of a file become characters.

slides.title: encoding: how bytes become characters
slides.say: A file stores bytes, and the encoding says how bytes become characters. The word café has four characters, but in UTF-8 the letter e with an accent takes two bytes, so the file holds five bytes: the bytes of caf and the two bytes with the values c3 and a9. The chart compares the counts. Reading the file with the same encoding that wrote it gives the word back; reading with another one gives wrong characters or an error. That is why every open call in this deck names UTF-8. Slide 19 told the story of how the character set was agreed.

slides.title: Part 4: Saving variables
slides.say: Part 4 keeps Python values between two runs of a program. A shelf is a dictionary that is kept in a file, with one value under each key, and json is a plain text format that other programs can read as well. The cards also carry a warning: a list changed in place is not saved, and a shelf that came from a stranger must never be opened. Slides 27 to 31 show both ways and the stories behind them. Part 5 puts everything to work in programs.

slides.title: Saving variables with shelve and json
slides.say: The headline defines the shelf: a file that is used like a dictionary and keeps its entries between two runs of a program. shelve.open() opens the shelf file and creates it when it does not exist, and the Shelf object is used with keys and values. json is a plain-text format that programs in many languages can read, which is the reason to choose it when another program has to read your data. Slide 28 runs the shelf, and slide 30 runs json.

slides.title: shelve: a dictionary that a file can keep
slides.say: The shelve module keeps Python values in a file, so that the next run of a program finds them again. Shelve.open opens a file, here mydata, and the shelf works like a dictionary: the program stores a list under the key cats. After closing, it opens the shelf again and prints its type, which is DbfilenameShelf, its keys, which are the single word cats, and the list itself. The values survived the closing of the program's file. The table on the slide lists what was read back. A shelf can hold lists and dictionaries, but not every kind of object. Slide 29 explains what is behind the file, and slide 30 shows a plain-text way of saving values.

slides.title: Story: a shelf rests on a 1979 Bell Labs idea
slides.say: In 1979 Ken Thompson, a programmer at AT&T Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, wrote the first dbm, a small store that keeps a value under a text key. AT&T released it as part of Unix. A program needed to save a value and get it back by one key, with no server to run. That one-key, one-value shape is still what a Python dbm file offers today. shelve.open() gives the same shape, and Python's dbm package picks the backend file that holds your values, as slide 28 shows.

slides.title: json: a plain format other programs read
slides.say: Json writes the same kind of data as plain text that programs in other languages can read, which a shelf file cannot offer. The program makes a dictionary with a list inside it. Dumps turns it into text with double quotation marks, and the program prints that text. Loads turns the text back into a dictionary, and the comparison with the original is True. The table shows both steps. A json text can be stored in a file with write_text and sent over a network. Not every Python value fits: a tuple comes back as a list, and keys must be text, which is the price of a format that every language understands. Part 5, the practice programs, begins with slide 31.

slides.title: Story: why Windows calls the main drive C:
slides.say: Gary Kildall demonstrated CP/M in 1974 in Pacific Grove, California, and it named each floppy drive with a letter. MS-DOS began as a CP/M look-alike that Microsoft licensed from Seattle Computer Products, so the letters came along. The letters A and B went to the floppy drives, which is why a hard disk received the next free letter, C. Windows is no longer built on MS-DOS, but its paths still start with a drive letter, such as C:\Users. Slide 10 takes a Windows path apart and shows the drive as one part of it, and the drive attribute of a Windows path returns it. The link opens a short article on how drive letters began.

slides.title: Part 5: Programs
slides.say: Part 5 has two practice programs and Project 4 of the book, the quiz maker. Mad Libs fills the blanks of a story file with re.sub, Regex Search finds a pattern in every text file of a folder, and Project 4 writes quiz files and answer keys at random. Each program uses only what parts 1 to 4 taught: paths, glob, reading, writing and a little randomness. Slides 33 to 37 follow, and slide 38 lists what current Python adds.

slides.title: Chapter programs and practice work
slides.say: The headline says what the programs of this chapter have in common: they read files, change the text and write a new file. Project 4 writes a different quiz file for each student, Mad Libs replaces the placeholder words of a story from a text file, and Regex Search prints the matching lines of every text file in a folder. The practice programs repeat the same steps until they are familiar, and the practice questions on slide 40 are short exercises that each have their answer on an earlier slide.

slides.title: Practice program: Mad Libs
slides.say: The Mad Libs program reads a story from a file, replaces its capital-letter words with answers, and saves the new story. The story has the words ADJECTIVE, NOUN, VERB and NOUN. The loop takes the words in order, and replace with a count of one swaps only the first match each time, so the second NOUN receives the fourth answer. The answers come from a list, because the book's version asks the user to type them. The program prints the finished story and writes it to panda_filled.txt. The text box on the slide shows the saved story. The program reads one file and writes another, which is the pattern of most file programs. Slide 35 searches several files at once.

slides.title: Practice program: search the text files
slides.say: This practice program searches every text file of a folder for lines that match a pattern. Glob lists the files ending in .txt in sorted order, and the file notes.csv is left out because its name does not match. For each file the program reads the text, splits it into lines with splitlines, and numbers them with enumerate, starting at one. A compiled pattern tests each line, and a hit prints the file name, the line number and the line. The pattern spam finds a.txt line 1 and b.txt line 2; the line with SPAM in capitals is not matched, because patterns are case-sensitive unless told otherwise. The table lists the two hits. Regular expressions are the subject of chapter 9.

slides.title: Project 4, step 1: one multiple-choice question
slides.say: Project 4 of the book generates quizzes with the capitals of states. Step one makes a single question. The dictionary holds four states and their capitals, and the fixed seed in random.seed makes the shuffle repeat, so the same question appears on every run: the capital of Maine. The program shuffles the states, takes the first, remembers the right capital, shuffles the four capitals into options, and prints them with the letters A to D. The table marks the right option. The book uses fifty states and removes the right capital from the wrong ones first; with four states all four capitals serve as options. Step two, on slide 37, writes the quiz and its key to files.

slides.title: Project 4, step 2: write the quiz and its key
slides.say: Step two of Project 4 writes the quiz and its answer key into two files, as the book does. The loop makes one question for each state: the question line and its four options go to the quiz file, and the number with the right letter goes to the key file. The right letter is found with options.index, which gives the position of the right capital in the shuffled list. Both files are closed at the end, and the program prints them. The table shows the key, one letter for each question. The book writes thirty-five quizzes of fifty questions; the structure is the same. Slide 38 looks at what current Python adds to file work.

slides.title: What differs from the book today
slides.say: The table lists seven things from the chapter that current Python changes, and the last column says on which slide the chapter's own example is. Python 3.12 adds Path.walk and a case_sensitive option for glob, and it deprecates st_ctime on Windows. Python 3.14 makes exists, is_file and is_dir return False instead of raising any OSError. Python 3.13 makes dbm.sqlite3 the first shelve backend, Python 3.10 adds EncodingWarning, and Python 3.15 makes UTF-8 mode the default. The examples are on slides 13, 14, 15, 25 and 28. Running what the book printed and then checking what changed is the safest habit.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: The five numbered sentences are the chapter in one line each, and they answer the first question of slide 3: Path() and the slash compute, exists, glob and stat ask, and makedirs, writing and shelve change. The chart counts the code examples in each part: three in part 1, three in part 2, six in part 3, two in part 4 and four in part 5, eighteen in all. Each sentence keeps only the point that must be remembered, and each can be traced to a slide. Chapter 11 builds on all of it.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: The four questions are short exercises. Each can be answered in a few lines that you run on the chapter page. The first asks why the slash works when a path stands on its left and fails for two strings; slide 6 answers it. The second asks what the file holds after the modes w, a, a, w and what mode x does; slide 24 answers it. The third asks why a list changed inside a shelf is lost and how to keep the change: edit the shelve program of slide 28, change the list in place, close the shelf and read it again. The fourth asks for the key file to name the right capital as well: edit the program of slide 37. Predict the answer first and then run it.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: The cards collect the further reading for this chapter, and every link is live. They begin with the book chapter and the Python documentation of pathlib, open, io, shelve, dbm, json and tempfile, continue with the proposals behind pathlib, UTF-8 mode and the encoding warning, and end with first-hand sources for the stories and a video on file objects. Choose one link and read it before the next class. The stories on slides 7, 19, 29 and 31 link to their own sources.
